When Wars Move Markets

How the 2026 US–Iran war, Red Sea attacks and a sanctions war on Russian energy travelled through the world’s shipping chokepoints into oil and gas prices — and from there into inflation, interest rates and growth forecasts.

By Bhargav Patel Compiled 12 October 2026 Coverage 2024–2026 data, latest figures to 9 October 2026 Sources IMF · World Bank · UNCTAD · OECD · IEA · EIA · Drewry · Freightos · FAO · AAA
STEP 1

US–Iran war from 28 Feb 2026; Houthi attacks in the Red Sea since Nov 2023; Russia–Ukraine war and sanctions.

01

Five flashpoints, one transmission belt

The world economy does not import “geopolitics” in the abstract. It imports oil, gas, grain and containerised goods through a handful of narrow sea lanes — and in 2026, several of those lanes are blocked, mined, sanctioned or running dry at the same time.

The dominant shock is the US–Iran war that began on 28 February 2026, which disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, the channel for roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas. But it landed on a system already weakened: Houthi attacks had kept most container shipping out of the Red Sea since late 2023, the Russia–Ukraine war and sanctions were still squeezing grain, energy and fertiliser flows, drought had cut capacity at the Panama Canal, and tensions around Taiwan kept the world’s semiconductor supply under a standing question mark.

Active · Energy chokepoint

Strait of Hormuz — the war’s chokehold

After US–Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran declared the strait closed; the IRGC banned merchant vessels and laid mines. Before the crisis, about 20.9 million barrels a day — roughly 20% of global petroleum liquids — plus more than 20% of global LNG passed through it. (skn-finance.com)

  • Flows fell from 21.6 mb/d in Q4 2025 to 14.9 mb/d in Q1 2026 and just 4.9 mb/d in Q2 2026. (EIA data)
  • Workarounds rebuilt much of the crude flow: 16.5 mb/d exited the Middle East in September, near pre-war ex-Iran levels, with ~40% of regional crude now bypassing the strait via Saudi and Emirati pipelines, up from 17% pre-war. (Kpler, 1–2 Oct 2026)
  • Refined products — diesel above all — remain heavily constrained even though crude has partly recovered.
  • Iran’s own crude exports fell ~90%, to 260–300k b/d. (Cryptobriefing, Aug 2026)
  • As of 8 October, Hormuz transits had hit a two-month low, and the IRGC threatened to block “illegal” routes off the Omani coast — an unverified Iranian government claim. (7–8 Oct 2026 reports)

The Hormuz squeeze

Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, million barrels per day (EIA data)

Crude flows later partly recovered through pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers — Kpler put total Middle East exports at 16.5 mb/d in September — but that figure covers all exit routes, not the strait alone, and diesel flows stayed tight. See “Where the numbers disagree” below.

Active since Nov 2023 · Container chokepoint

Red Sea & Suez — the long way around Africa

Houthi attacks on shipping — 99 ships attacked or hijacked, per Lloyd’s List — pushed most Asia–Europe container traffic around the Cape of Good Hope. Suez transits by deadweight tonnage ran 57–64% below 2023 through 2025, and container transits were 86% below in Q4 2025. (BIMCO, Sept 2026) War-risk insurance premiums rose from 0.05% to 1% of hull value. Egypt’s canal revenue fell from $10.2B in 2023 to roughly $4B, recovering to $4.67B in FY2025/26. (Planning minister Ahmed Rostom, 8 Oct 2026)

A tentative return in early 2026 was derailed by the Iran war and renewed Houthi action over the summer. On 14 September 2026 Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd resumed four more Suez services — about a third of Asia–Europe sailings, and conditional.

“During 2025, Suez Canal DWT transits have been 57–64% lower than in 2023.”

Niels Rasmussen, chief shipping analyst, BIMCO (via infomarine.net, ~Jan 2026)
Active · Food & energy sanctions

Russia–Ukraine — grain, gas and the shadow fleet

  • Ukraine’s grain exports fell 75% in the first two weeks of August 2026 versus a year earlier. (Reuters) Kyiv School of Economics puts direct agricultural losses at $12.1B and revenue losses at $81.9B for 2022–2025; farm products are up to 60% of Ukraine’s export earnings.
  • Russia suspended its floating grain export duty through 31 Dec 2026 after Ukrainian strikes disrupted Black Sea and Azov routes covering over 70% of its exports. (Bloomberg Law, Sept 2026)
  • The EU’s 19th sanctions package (adopted 23 Oct 2025) bans Russian LNG imports from 25 Apr 2026 for short-term contracts and 1 Jan 2027 for long-term ones; the 20th package (23 Apr 2026) laid the basis for a maritime services ban on Russian crude and products, with 632 vessels now designated. (Council of the EU; P&I club circulars)
Latent · Semiconductors

Taiwan Strait — the risk that hasn’t fired yet

  • 208 PLA sorties around Taiwan in June 2026; PRC coast guard and naval operations up 89% in early 2026 versus late 2025. (theworldreviews.com, Oct 2026)
  • Trade is not yet broadly disrupted — Taiwan’s exports hit $74.8B in June 2026, up 40.3% year on year — but TSMC chairman Mark Liu has warned that military force would make the fabs non-operable: “a war brings no winners.”
  • The exposure is doubled: Taiwan takes ~33.7% of its LNG from Qatar, tying chip supply directly to Hormuz risk. (Resilinc, Aug 2026)
Strained · Climate, not conflict

Panama Canal — drought rationing

  • Daily transits cut from 36 to 32 from 15 Sept 2026, rising back to 33 from 15 Oct; in August some vessels waited up to 10 days, and one reportedly paid ~$4M to skip the queue. (informat.ro, Sept 2026)
  • Carrier surcharges followed: MSC $297 per 40ft box, CMA CGM $500 per TEU. The canal carries ~5% of global maritime trade and ~40% of US container traffic.
02

The freight bill: longer routes, doubled rates

Rerouting is not free. Every Asia–Europe ship that rounds the Cape of Good Hope instead of transiting Suez adds 10–14 days at sea — and someone pays for the fuel, the crew and the lost capacity. In 2026, that someone is the importer, and ultimately the shopper.

Transit times from Asia to Europe are up 25–33%, and to the US East Coast up 47%; container ton-miles — the shipping system’s total workload — are up 17%, and tanker ton-miles 7.5%. (knowafrika.com) Carriers layered emergency fuel surcharges on top once the Iran war began: CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd charged $70–75 per TEU regionally and $150 per TEU on long-haul routes from 23 March. (Freightos)

The result: the Drewry World Container Index, the standard spot benchmark, went from $2,107 per 40ft container in late January 2026 to $4,351 on 8 October — and on 1 October it stood 166% above its level a year earlier. (Drewry)

Container spot rates roughly doubled in 2026

Drewry World Container Index, US$ per 40ft container (Drewry; mid-Sept figure via Xeneta reporting)

Drewry notes Asia–Europe spot rates have now fallen for 12–13 consecutive weeks as some Suez sailings resume, and calls a faster-than-expected Suez return “the biggest threat to carrier efforts to support rates.” Intra-Asia rates, meanwhile, hit an all-time high for six straight weeks on typhoons and port congestion.

03

Energy: the price of a closed strait

Oil is the fastest wire between a battlefield and a household budget. It took eight days from the first strikes for Brent crude to break $100 a barrel — and it has stayed near or above that line ever since.

Before the war, Brent averaged about $69 a barrel in February 2026, in a $69–77 range. It broke $100 on 8 March; how high it peaked is genuinely disputed — secondary estimates put the peak at $120, $126 or $138 (7 April, per OECD analysis). In May it swung between $102 and $114 within single sessions. WTI touched $105.63 in September, its first time above $100 since May. By 8 October Brent was back to $101.53 and WTI to $89.39, lifted again by fears of attacks on Gulf tankers. (Reuters via informat.ro; Trading Economics)

Governments responded with the largest fire brigade in oil-market history: the IEA’s coordinated release of 400 million barrels from strategic reserves on 11 March 2026 — the biggest in the agency’s history — followed by a G7 agreement on 2–3 October to release another 100 million barrels of diesel and crude and to refrain from energy export restrictions. The US strategic stockpile, meanwhile, sits at its lowest level in more than 40 years. The IEA estimates more than 14 mb/d of Gulf output was shut in during May and cumulative conflict supply losses passed 1 billion barrels; it now expects 2026 global oil demand to fall by 1.56 mb/d — destruction caused by the price itself. (IEA Oil Market Report, Aug 2026, via Argus)

Brent crude: from $69 to triple digits in eight days

Reported reference points, 2026, US$ per barrel — not a continuous price series

Points are the specific values reported by the cited sources: February pre-war average (~$69), the 8 March break above $100, the disputed spring peak (whisker shows the $120–$138 range of estimates), May’s intraday range (midpoint plotted), and the 8 October close of $101.53 (Reuters). The EIA’s October Short-Term Energy Outlook averages Brent at $96 for 2026 as a whole and $84 for 2027.

Gas: a two-tier market

If oil is one global price, gas is now two markets moving apart. Europe’s TTF benchmark started 2026 near €41/MWh, averaged €63.69 in Q2, and peaked at €84/MWh in early-to-mid September — the highest since December 2022 — before easing to €74–76 in early October, still up 78–83% year to date. The trigger chain ran through Hormuz again: Qatar, source of ~20% of global LNG exports, declared force majeure on 4 March after drone attacks on its facilities, and September LNG volumes through the strait reached only ~25% of pre-war levels despite hitting a wartime record. (TechTimes, 2 Oct 2026; Elenger Q3 overview)

Europe enters winter exposed: storage is ~68–71% full against a five-year seasonal average of 84–87% — the lowest volume since 2013 — and the European Commission has cut the mandatory winter target from 90% to 80%. The US, by contrast, is insulated: Henry Hub sits near $3/MMBtu with decade-high storage. (TradingNews)

European gas (TTF): up ~80% in 2026

Dutch TTF benchmark, €/MWh, reported reference points

Bank forecasts for Q4 2026 diverge: UBS €75, Rabobank €60 average, Oxford Economics ~€60 — while Goldman Sachs warns December TTF could exceed €100/MWh if normalisation is gradual. Rabobank’s Florence Schmit: “only a credible political agreement that restores shipping confidence can remove the structural risk premium from TTF.”

04

From the pump to the price tag

Energy is an input to almost everything — freight, fertiliser, food processing, heating, flying. So an energy shock does not stay in the energy statistics. By the autumn of 2026 it was in the grocery index, in the inflation prints, and in the policy rates of the world’s major central banks.

At the pump the shock is unmissable. US gasoline averaged $4.36 a gallon on 8 October — a record high for autumn and the first October ever above $4, against $3.12 a year earlier; September’s monthly average of $4.33 smashed the previous September record of $3.83. Diesel reached $6.20 a gallon. (AAA, 8 Oct 2026; EIA, 5 Oct 2026) In Canada, regular gasoline averaged $1.68 a litre on 13 August. (Burnabyhouse / IEA reporting, Aug 2026)

Food followed energy, as it usually does — through fertiliser prices, transport costs and Black Sea logistics. The FAO Food Price Index reached 136.0 in September 2026, its highest in about four years, up 5.8% year on year, with cereals up 17.2% year on year and vegetable oils at their highest since June 2022. It remains below the March 2022 peak of 160.2 — but the direction is what worries the FAO’s chief economist:

“August’s increase in global food prices is a warning that the risk premium is returning to food markets: climate shocks, geopolitical tensions and disrupted trade logistics are converging to tighten supply expectations.”

Maximo Torero, chief economist, FAO (Sept 2026)

The inflation prints forced central banks to reverse direction. In September 2026 the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan all raised rates — the classic signature of a supply shock, where policymakers must fight inflation even as growth weakens. US CPI rose 3.4% year on year in August, with gasoline up 3.9% in the month alone; euro-area inflation hit 3.2–3.3%, with energy up 14.3% year on year and contributing 1.29 percentage points. ECB staff attribute roughly 90% of the January–May rise in energy inflation to adverse supply factors — not demand. And the ECB’s October minutes warn that “the full inflationary impact of the energy shock had yet to play out.” ECB President Lagarde has said inflation is “set to remain well above target for an extended period.”

The burden is not shared evenly. IMF research published 6 October 2026 finds cost-of-living crises are becoming more frequent and hit poorer households hardest: its new model shows a 0.8-percentage-point gap for poorer households translates into 23 million more people below the extreme poverty line in 2021–2024 than previously calculated. As IMF economist Chiara Maggi put it: “In a nutshell, cost-of-living crises … impact price stability, they reduce living standards and they worsen inequality.” (Reuters, 6 Oct 2026)

05

What forecasters expect next

Every major forecaster has cut 2026 growth — but they were all, to different degrees, pricing in a war that ends. The forecasts below were made at different dates with different assumptions about Hormuz, which is why they disagree, and why the IMF’s full October outlook — due the week of 12–16 October and not yet published — matters so much.

2026 global growth forecasts — all cut, none catastrophic (yet)

Real GDP growth, % · Forecast date in brackets · Dashed line: 2024–25 average of 3.5% (IMF)

The IMF’s July update pairs 3.0% growth with 4.7% inflation for 2026 (revised from April’s 3.1% and 4.4%), with the US at 2.3%, the euro area at 1.1%, China 4.4%, India 6.5% — and Iran at −6.1%. UNCTAD (9 Oct) notes world trade in goods and services still grew 4% in constant prices, but driven by higher energy prices rather than volumes of prosperity. The World Bank’s worst case is 1.3%.

The spread between institutions is really a spread of assumptions. Try the IMF’s own scenario ladder:

3.0% global growth, 2026

“In effect, we expect a V-shaped recovery, weaker growth this year relative to our pre-war forecast, followed by a rebound next year. The world economy has weathered the shock from the war better than feared so far, with limited evidence of second round effects.”

Petya Koeva Brooks, IMF deputy research director, July 2026 briefing

That was July — and the July forecast assumed the Strait of Hormuz would start reopening in mid-July and normalise by March 2027. It did not. The stagflation warning is now explicit in market commentary: J.P. Morgan’s James Sullivan argues that “a sustained rise in oil prices above $100 a barrel risks marking the start of a stagflation period, even if overall growth does not slow significantly” (via CNBC, ~25 Sept 2026). Goldman Sachs argues $80–90 a barrel becomes a “new floor” for oil regardless of how Hormuz resolves, because the geopolitical risk premium has been permanently repriced — though that claim reaches us second-hand and should be weighted accordingly. The IEA’s arithmetic cuts both ways: with de-escalation, a 4 mb/d supply overhang from Q4 2026 could rebuild stocks to February 2026 levels by mid-2027; without it, the structural deficit persists. One widely-circulated forecast (LongForecast, 8 Oct) has Brent at ~$101 through October–November and $107.45 by December.

The World Bank’s Franziska Ohnsorge adds a timing warning: in emerging markets, “the normal lag between such shocks and their effect on economic activity is around 18 months” — meaning much of the growth damage from 2026’s prices may not arrive until 2027. (Reuters, 6 Oct 2026)

Regions most exposed

  • Europe — energy-import dependent, with the tightest winter gas position since 2022; Germany’s storage association warns a cold winter could leave demand uncovered in full.
  • Asia — 84% of Hormuz crude goes to China, India, Japan and South Korea; Taiwan’s chip economy also leans on Qatari LNG.
  • Oil-importing sub-Saharan Africa & South Asia — food and energy prices bite hardest where budgets are thinnest; the World Bank still expects SSA growth of 4.3% and raised South Asia to 6.9%.
  • Egypt — Suez revenue roughly halved from its $10.2B peak.
  • Gulf producers & Iran — shut-in output on one side; an economy forecast to shrink 6.1% on the other.

Sectors most exposed

  • Transport & logistics — fuel surcharges, rerouting, war-risk premiums.
  • Airlines — cancelled flights and jet-fuel costs.
  • Chemicals & fertilisers — the Gulf supplies roughly 30–35% of global urea exports (single-source figure; see caveats), feeding directly into food prices.
  • Agriculture & food processing — FAO index at a four-year high.
  • Refining — diesel remains the tightest product even as crude recovers.
  • Diesel-dependent small businesses — least able to hedge or pass costs on.

And the war economy does not operate in a vacuum. Forecasters flag a severe El Niño, European heatwaves and drought, US tariff-driven trade fragmentation (China–US trade is down more than 20% since 2024), and the risk of an AI-market correction as compounding shocks. The mechanism, though, is already in motion: a war closes a strait, the strait reprices energy, energy reprices everything else — and central banks are left choosing which kind of pain to administer.

06

Where the numbers disagree

Open questions & contested figures — read these before citing

  • How high did oil actually peak? Secondary estimates differ — $120 (9 Mar), $126, and $138 (7 Apr, per OECD analysis). All agree Brent broke $100 in early March and stayed elevated; this article treats peak figures as approximate.
  • How recovered is Hormuz? Kpler-based reporting puts ~16.5 mb/d exiting the Middle East in September (all routes, including pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers), while August reporting had regional exports roughly halved to ~9.5 mb/d with strait traffic at 2–9 mb/d. Different metrics and dates explain part — not all — of the gap.
  • The IMF’s July baseline is stale. It assumed Hormuz would begin reopening in mid-July 2026 and normalise by March 2027. Escalation since then has invalidated that assumption; the October WEO (due the week of 12–16 Oct 2026) had not been published when this brief was compiled.
  • Euro-area August inflation is reported as 3.2% by LSEG and 3.3% by ainvest.
  • Two claims rest on thinner sourcing: Goldman Sachs’ $80–90 “new floor” for oil arrives second-hand via a low-quality aggregator, and the Gulf’s ~30–35% share of urea exports comes from a single low-quality source — though ECB minutes corroborate the fertiliser-price mechanism qualitatively.
  • Method note: the underlying research was gathered on 12 Oct 2026 from search-index results and official pages, not verified in a live browser session. Figures are reported as their sources state them; where a number matters, check the primary source.
Still to come: the full October 2026 IMF World Economic Outlook, including a dedicated cost-of-living chapter, is due the week of 12–16 October 2026. It is expected to revise the July forecasts quoted here — this page will need those numbers replaced, not supplemented, once it lands.
